Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slopes become vertical as $y\to -2$ only. 

Of the given equations, the only equations that satisfy this condition are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{(y+2)^{2}} \\ {y}^{′} & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{y+2} \\ {y}^{′} & =-\frac{3}{y+2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Second, the slopes become horizontal as $y\to \infty .$

Of the remaining options, the only two that give this behavior are

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{(y+2)^{2}} \\ {y}^{′} & =-\frac{3}{y+2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, the slopes of the slope field are positive for all $y\ne -2.$ 

Therefore, the equation ${y}^{′}=-\frac{3}{y+2}$ does *not* give the required behavior. The slopes of the slope field for this differential equation are negative for $y>-2.$

On the other hand, the equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{(y+2)^{2}}$ gives the required behavior. Notice that the right-hand side of this equation is positive for all $y\ne -2.$

So, the correct answer is ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{(y+2)^{2}}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Generalized Eigenvectors of a 3x3 Matrix
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 6 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}],\,v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $v$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true?

- $v$ is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ of $A$
- $v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ of $A$
- $v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ of $A$
questions.worked_solution:
A *generalized eigenvector* ${v}_{n}$ of rank $n$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda $ of a matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector such that

$$
{v}_{n}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{n-1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }…\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }0,
$$

where ${v}_{n-1},{v}_{n-2},…,{v}_{1}\ne 0.$ An *eigenvector* is simply a generalized eigenvector of rank $1.$

First, we compute $A-4I:$

$$
A-4I=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 6 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

- Next, we find the image of $v$ under the action of $A-4I:$

$$
(A-4I)v=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{w}\ne 0
$$

- Since we got a nonzero vector in the last step, we now compute the image of $w$ under the action of $A-4I:$

$$
(A-4I)w=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=0
$$

So, we obtain the following chain of maps:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{v}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{w}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{0}
$$

Here, we see that $A-4I$ maps $v$ to $0$ in $2$ steps.

Therefore:

$\,$ *$v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ of $A.$*

So, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Inhomogeneous System of Linear ODEs Using Variation of Parameters
questions.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -6 & 5\end{aligned}]x(t)+[\begin{aligned}2t \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the system of differential equations. Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form

| $x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+\,\,\frac{1}{9}$ |  | $30t-26$ |  | . |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-1}} |  |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & {e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{-t} & 3{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}2t \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-t}\cdot 3{e}^{3t}-{e}^{3t}\cdot {e}^{-t}}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{2t}}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2t \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3t{e}^{t} \\ -t{e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}3t{e}^{t} \\ -t{e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 3t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -t{e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=3t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=3\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =(3t)\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\cdot (3\,\text{d}t) \\  & =3t{e}^{t}-3{e}^{t} \\  & =3{e}^{t}(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=-t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -t{e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t & =(-t)\cdot (-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t})-\int (-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t})\cdot (-\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{t}{3}{e}^{-3t}-\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{t}{3}{e}^{-3t}+\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t}(3t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & {e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{-t} & 3{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3{e}^{t}(t-1) \\ \frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t}(3t+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}27(t-1)+(3t+1) \\ 27(t-1)+3(3t+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}30t-26 \\ 36t-24\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+5y=f(x),\,y(0)=0,\,y(1)=4
$$

where $f(x)$ is $1$-periodic and odd. Select the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0.$*

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We write the solution as $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}$, where ${y}_{c}$ solves the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation ${y}^{″}+5y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0$, we have

$$
y(0)={y}_{c}(0)\,\text{and}\,y(1)={y}_{c}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions.

- Use $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+B(0)+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{c}(x)=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x).$

- Use $y(1)=4$ with $A=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})+{y}_{p}(1) \\ 4 & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})+0 \\ B & =\frac{4}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼\frac{4}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$

questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t)y(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-2x(t)-y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the behavior of the system's solutions near the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}?$$\,$
The equilibrium is an 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}xy+y \\ -2x-y\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+y)=y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+y)=x+1 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2x-y)=-2,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2x-y)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}y & x+1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-\lambda  & 1 \\ -2 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(-1-\lambda )-(-2)(1) & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda +1)+2 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda +2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-\frac{1}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{2}\text{i}.$

Finally, since we have two complex eigenvalues with negative real parts, our equilibrium is an $\text{asymptotically stable}$ $\text{spiral sink}.$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14097559/assets/5322f43ff1eeee6e06b3c393cc1b59c9af32bc2e7dba66766607af117954ace1.png)

Find, in amperes, the amplitude of the steady state current for the RCL circuit shown above.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $8\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $20\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.1\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $10\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=20\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=20I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.1}=10q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=10\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=10\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
8\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)=20I+10q+10\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(8\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(20I+10q+10\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ -8\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =20\,\frac{dI}{dt}+10\,\frac{dq}{dt}+10\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}+I=-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+Bt{e}^{-t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find a particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute this, as well as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t))+2(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)) \\ +(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)) & =-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ (2\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+(-2\alpha )\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)) \\ -2\alpha =-\frac{4}{5}\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{2}{5}$ and $\beta =0.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+Bt{e}^{-t}+\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+Bt{e}^{-t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${I}_{p}(t)=\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{(\frac{2}{5})}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=\frac{2}{5}.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the inexact differential equation

$$
xy\,\text{d}x-({x}^{2}+3{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y=0.
$$

It is known that 

$$
\frac{1}{P}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x})=\frac{3}{y}
$$

where the functions $P$ and $Q$ are given by 

$$
P(x,y)=xy,\,Q(x,y)=-{x}^{2}-3{y}^{3}.
$$

Use this information to find a suitable integrating factor $I(y)$ and hence find the general solution to the equation.

$\,$ A suitable integrating factor is $I(y)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is {{field-2}}, where $c$ is a constant.
questions.worked_solution:
For a differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y=0,
$$

we have that if

$$
\frac{1}{P}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x})=h(y)
$$

where $h(y)$ is independent of $x,$ then an integrating factor for the equation is

$$
I(y)=\operatorname{exp}⁡(-\int h(y)\,\text{d}y)
$$

where $\operatorname{exp}⁡(y)$ denotes the exponential function ${e}^{y}.$

We are given that

$$
\frac{1}{P}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x})=\frac{3}{y}.
$$

Since $\frac{3}{y}$ is a function of $y$ only, we can conclude that the integrating factor for the equation is 

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x,y) & ={e}^{-\int 3/y\text{ }\text{d}y} \\  & ={e}^{-3\operatorname{ln}⁡y} \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying our equation by the integrating factor, we arrive at the following exact differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{y}^{3}}(xy\,\text{d}x-({x}^{2}+3{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y) & =0 \\ {{(\frac{x}{{y}^{2}})}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{P}}\,\text{d}x+{{(-1)(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{3}}+3)}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{Q}}\,\text{d}y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

For this exact equation, we have

$$
\overset{~}{P}(x,y)=\frac{x}{{y}^{2}},\,\overset{~}{Q}(x,y)=-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{3}}-3.
$$

To solve the equation, let's first integrate $\overset{~}{P}(x,y)$ with respect to $x.$
The result should include an arbitrary function of $y,$ which we'll call $F(y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int \overset{~}{P}(x,y)\,\text{d}x+F(y) \\  & =\int \frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+F(y) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{y}^{2}}+F(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, let's integrate $\overset{~}{Q}(x,y)$ with respect to $y.$
The result should include an arbitrary function of $x,$ which we'll call $G(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int \overset{~}{Q}(x,y)\,\text{d}y+G(x) \\  & =\int (-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{3}}-3)\,\text{d}y+G(x) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{y}^{2}}-3y+G(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing the two solutions, we see that we must have

$$
F(y)=-3y,\,G(x)=0.
$$

Therefore, the general solution $u(x,y)=c$ is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{y}^{2}}-3y=c.
$$

questions.problem:
A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The position of the particle $y(t)$ at time $t$ is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+16y=32t.
$$

Which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for $y(t)?$

- $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+ϕ)+16t$
- $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+2t$
- $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡4t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+8t$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R$ and $ϕ$ are constants.
questions.worked_solution:
The general solution is the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution:

$$
y(t)={y}_{c}(t)+{y}_{p}(t)
$$

First, we find the complementary solution ${y}_{c}(t),$ which is the solution to the simple harmonic motion equation ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=0.$ It can be written in three different forms:

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)$

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)$

- ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t$

In our case

$$
{\omega }^{2}=16\,⟹\,\omega =4.
$$

Thus, we have:

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

- ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡4t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡4t$

Next, we find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t).$ Since the external force is a linear function, we assume that the particular solution is also a linear function,

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\alpha t+\beta .
$$

By substituting the particular solution into the differential equation and equating coefficients, we find that $\alpha =2$ and $\beta =0.$ So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=2t.
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)+2t, \\ y(t) & =R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+2t, \\ y(t) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡4t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡4t+2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Only II matches the forms above. Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

questions.problem:
Find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ of the equation 

$$
{x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-3x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3y=9\operatorname{ln}⁡x,\,x>0.

questions.worked_solution:
This Cauchy-Euler equation has non-polynomial forcing, but we are not given two fundamental solutions, so we cannot use variation of parameters.

However, if we make a substitution $x={e}^{t},$ we can transform the Cauchy-Euler equation into a linear ODE with constant coefficients.

Letting $x={e}^{t},$ we note that

$$

$$

Then, we use the chain rule to compute the first and second derivatives. 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}, \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\  & ={{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x})\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}_{⏟}}_{\text{product rule}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot {{\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}}_{⏟}}_{\text{chain rule}}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+3y=9t.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is a second-order inhomogeneous differential equation with constant coefficients and polynomial forcing. 

Using the usual methods for solving second-order ODEs, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{t}+B{e}^{3t}.
$$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.,

$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}t}=\alpha ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}=0.
$$

$$
0-4\alpha +3(\alpha t+\beta )=9t

$$

$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}3\alpha =9\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of }t) \\ 3\beta -4\alpha =0\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\alpha =3$ and $\beta =4,$ and so the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=3t+4.
$$

Now, returning to the variable $x,$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=3\operatorname{ln}⁡x+4.
$$

$$

$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+3y=10\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is a second-order inhomogeneous differential equation with constant coefficients and sinusoidal forcing. 

Using the usual methods for solving second-order ODEs, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{t}+B{e}^{3t}.
$$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $10\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is

$$

questions.problem:
$$
{y}^{‴}-2{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}-8y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\,{{y}_{1}={e}^{2x},\,{y}_{2}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),\,{y}_{3}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}
$$

Consider the differential equation and the set of fundamental solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation above. 
Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form

$$
y(x)=A{e}^{2x}+B\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+C\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+{u}_{1}(x){e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+{u}_{3}(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

What is the function ${u}_{2}(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
According to the method of variation of parameters, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2}+{u}_{3}{y}_{3},\,{u}_{i}=(-1)^{3-i}\int \frac{g(x){W}_{i}(x)}{W(x)}\,\text{d}x,\,i=1,2,3,
$$

where $g(x)$ is the forcing term, $W(x)$ is the Wronskian of ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},{y}_{3},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}_{1}(x)=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{2} & {y}_{3} \\ {y}_{2}^{′} & {y}_{3}^{′}\end{aligned}|,\,{W}_{2}(x)=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{3} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{3}^{′}\end{aligned}|,\,{W}_{3}(x)=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, the forcing term is $g(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).$ Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions

$$
{y}_{1}={e}^{2x},\,{y}_{2}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),\,{y}_{3}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

First, let's verify that the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1},$ ${y}_{2},$ and ${y}_{3}$ are independent by computing the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W(x) & =W({y}_{1},{y}_{2},{y}_{3}) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{2x} & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) \\ 2{e}^{2x} & -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) \\ 4{e}^{2x} & -4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & -4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{2x}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) \\ 2 & -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) \\ 4 & -4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & -4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{2x}[(8{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+8{cos}^{2}⁡(2x))-2(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))+4(2{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+2{cos}^{2}⁡(2x))] \\  & ={e}^{2x}[8-2(0)+4(2)] \\  & =16{e}^{2x}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions ${y}_{1},$ ${y}_{2},$ and ${y}_{3}$ are linearly independent. 

Now, to find ${u}_{2},$ we compute the determinant ${W}_{2}(x)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}_{2}(x) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{3} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{3}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{2x} & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) \\ 2{e}^{2x} & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\end{aligned}| \\  & =2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) \\  & =2{e}^{2x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2}(x) & =(-1)^{3-2}\int \frac{g(x){W}_{2}(x)}{W(x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \frac{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))\cdot 2{e}^{2x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))}{16{e}^{2x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}\int [{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)-{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)]\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x) \\  & =-\frac{1}{32}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following differential equation.

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+(x+1)x{y}^{′}-4y=0
$$

The general solution near $x=0$ of the differential equation above is given by

$$
y={c}_{1}{x}^{2}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n}+{c}_{2}{y}_{2}(x),
$$

where ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ are arbitrary constants and ${a}_{n}$ are constants.
Which of the following is the form of the second Frobenius solution ${y}_{2},$ where the constants ${b}_{n}$ are determined by substitution?

*Hint: You may assume $x=0$ is a regular singular point of the ODE and the indicial equation of the ODE is ${\lambda }^{2}-4=0.$*
questions.worked_solution:
The general solution near a regular singular point $x=0$ of a second-order homogeneous linear differential equation with indicial roots ${\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}$ is given by

$$
y={c}_{1}{y}_{1}(x)+{c}_{2}{y}_{2}(x),
$$

where

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={x}^{{\lambda }_{1}}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}({\lambda }_{1}){x}^{n}
$$

is the first Frobenius solution, and the second Frobenius solution is determined as follows:

- **Case 1**: If ${\lambda }_{1}-{\lambda }_{2}\notin Z,$ then 
${y}_{2}(x)={x}^{{\lambda }_{2}}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}({\lambda }_{2}){x}^{n}.$

- **Case 2**: If ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2},$ then
${y}_{2}(x)={y}_{1}(x)\operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{{\lambda }_{1}}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{b}_{n}{x}^{n}.$

- **Case 3**: If ${\lambda }_{1}-{\lambda }_{2}\in N,$ then
${y}_{2}(x)={b}_{-1}{y}_{1}(x)\operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{{\lambda }_{2}}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{b}_{n}{x}^{n}.$

We are given that the indicial equation is ${\lambda }^{2}-4=0.$
Solving for the roots, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =4 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

The larger solution is ${\lambda }_{1}=2\ge -2={\lambda }_{2}.$ Therefore, the first Frobenius series solution we take is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={x}^{2}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n}.
$$

Now, since ${\lambda }_{1}-{\lambda }_{2}=2-(-2)=4$ *is* a positive integer, the other solution is given by

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={b}_{-1}{y}_{1}(x)\operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{-2}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{b}_{n}{x}^{n},
$$

where the constants ${b}_{n}$ are found by substitution.

questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+9{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,y(0)=y(\pi )=0,\,0\le x\le \pi ,\,\lambda \ge 0.
$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$ {{field-1}}, where $n\in N.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$
questions.worked_solution:
We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions $y(0)=y(\pi )=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ does not correspond to an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+9{\lambda }^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 3\text{i}\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\lambda x),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\lambda x)
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\lambda x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(0)=0$ yields

$$
A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $A=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(\pi )=0$ yields

$$
B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\lambda \pi )=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
3\lambda \pi =n\pi 
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{n}{3}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3{\lambda }_{n}x),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following differential equation.

$$
8{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+6x{y}^{′}+(8x-3)y=0
$$

Which of the following is a Frobenius series solution to the differential equation, where ${a}_{n}$ for $n=0,1,2,…$ are constants determined by substitution?

*Hint: Substituting a trial Frobenius series solution into each term of the ODE, we obtain*

$$
\begin{aligned}8{x}^{2}{y}^{″} & =8({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda ){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }8((\lambda +n)^{2}-(\lambda +n)){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}, \\ 6x{y}^{′} & =6\lambda {a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }6(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}, \\ (8x-3)y & =-3{a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(8{a}_{n-1}-3{a}_{n}){x}^{\lambda +n}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
If $x=0$ is a regular singular point of a second-order homogeneous linear differential equation, then the method of Frobenius states that there is at least one solution of the form

$$
y={x}^{\lambda }{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n},
$$

where $\lambda $ and ${a}_{n}$ for $n=0,1,2,…$ are constants.

Substituting this solution and its derivatives into the ODE, collecting like terms, and setting coefficients equal to zero, we obtain:

- the indicial equation from the coefficients of the $n=0$ term for arbitrary ${a}_{0},$ and

- a recurrence formula from the coefficients of the $n\ge 1$ terms.

We are given the three terms of the ODE as power series with the $n=0$ term isolated in each.

$$
\begin{aligned}8{x}^{2}{y}^{″} & =8({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda ){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }8((\lambda +n)^{2}-(\lambda +n)){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}, \\ 6x{y}^{′} & =6\lambda {a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }6(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n} \\ (8x-3)y & =-3{a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(8{a}_{n-1}-3{a}_{n}){x}^{\lambda +n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we continue from this point.

**Step 1**: Consolidate all the series into a single series that is equal to $0.$

Collecting the terms for $n=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}8({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda ){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+6\lambda {a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }-3{a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda } & = \\ (8{\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +6\lambda -3){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda } & = \\ (8{\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda } & .\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, collecting terms for $n\ge 1,$ we obtain an infinite series of the form
${x}^{\lambda }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(\lambda ){x}^{n},$
for some ${b}_{n}(\lambda ),$ $n\ge 1.$
Therefore, substituting into the homogeneous ODE, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(8{\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+{x}^{\lambda }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(\lambda ){x}^{n} & =0 \\ (8{\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3){a}_{0}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(\lambda ){x}^{n} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**:  Set the coefficients of the series equal to $0.$

Setting the coefficient of the $n=0$ term equal to $0$ with arbitrary ${a}_{0}\ne 0,$ we obtain the indicial equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(8{\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3){a}_{0} & =0 \\ 8{\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following differential equation.

$$
9{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+12x{y}^{′}+(9x-2)y=0
$$

Which of the following is a Frobenius series solution to the differential equation, where ${a}_{n}$ for $n=0,1,2,…$ are constants determined by substitution?

*Hint: Substituting a trial Frobenius series solution into each term of the ODE, we obtain*

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}{y}^{″} & =9({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda ){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }9((\lambda +n)^{2}-(\lambda +n)){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}, \\ 12x{y}^{′} & =12\lambda {a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }12(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}, \\ (9x-2)y & =-2{a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(9{a}_{n-1}-2{a}_{n}){x}^{\lambda +n}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
If $x=0$ is a regular singular point of a second-order homogeneous linear differential equation, then the method of Frobenius states that there is at least one solution of the form

$$
y={x}^{\lambda }{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n},
$$

where $\lambda $ and ${a}_{n}$ for $n=0,1,2,…$ are constants.

Substituting this solution and its derivatives into the ODE, collecting like terms, and setting coefficients equal to zero, we obtain:

- the indicial equation from the coefficients of the $n=0$ term for arbitrary ${a}_{0},$ and

- a recurrence formula from the coefficients of the $n\ge 1$ terms.

We are given the three terms of the ODE as power series with the $n=0$ term isolated in each.

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}{y}^{″} & =9({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda ){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }9((\lambda +n)^{2}-(\lambda +n)){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}, \\ 12x{y}^{′} & =12\lambda {a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }12(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}, \\ (9x-2)y & =-2{a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(9{a}_{n-1}-2{a}_{n}){x}^{\lambda +n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we continue from this point.

**Step 1**: Consolidate all the series into a single series that is equal to $0.$

Collecting the terms for $n=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}9({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda ){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+12\lambda {a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }-2{a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda } & = \\ (9{\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda +12\lambda -2){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda } & = \\ (9{\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -2){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda } & .\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, collecting terms for $n\ge 1,$ we obtain an infinite series of the form
${x}^{\lambda }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(\lambda ){x}^{n},$
for some ${b}_{n}(\lambda ),$ $n\ge 1.$
Therefore, substituting into the homogeneous ODE, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(9{\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -2){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+{x}^{\lambda }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(\lambda ){x}^{n} & =0 \\ (9{\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -2){a}_{0}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(\lambda ){x}^{n} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**:  Set the coefficients of the series equal to $0.$

Setting the coefficient of the $n=0$ term equal to $0$ with arbitrary ${a}_{0}\ne 0,$ we obtain the indicial equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(9{\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -2){a}_{0} & =0 \\ 9{\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can determine a solution. Solving the indicial equation for the roots, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}9{\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (3\lambda -1)(3\lambda +2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the two Frobenius series solutions are

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x)={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n-2/3}\,\text{and}\,y(x)={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n+1/3},\end{aligned}
$$

where the constants ${a}_{n}$ are to be determined separately in each of the two cases.

Of the given options, the correct answer is
$y(x)={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n+1/3}.$

$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & ={{field-4}}(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & ={{field-6}}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ & =A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =A(t)-A(0) \\  & =A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ} & =L{A(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & \,⇒\, & du={A}^{′}(t)\,dt \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A(0)=0$ and $\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ we have $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=0$ and

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{1}{s}\cdot F(s) \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+3y=\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,y(0)=1
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below to find the solution using Laplace transforms. You may make use of the following results:

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,s>0.
$$

Let $Y(s)=L{y(t)}.$ Taking the Laplace transform of both sides of the equation and solving for $Y,$ we have

$$
Y(s)={{field-1}}.
$$

The partial fraction decomposition of $Y$ is

$$
Y(s)={{field-2}}.
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t)={{field-3}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides of the differential equation. Using the linearity property, we have

$$
L{{y}^{′}}+3L{y}=L{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}+L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}.
$$

Using the formula for the transform of a derivative $L{{y}^{′}}=sY(s)-y(0)$ and the standard trigonometric transforms

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}=\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4},\,L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4},
$$

we substitute the known values. Note that $y(0)=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(sY(s)-1)+3Y(s) & =\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}+\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4} \\ (s+3)Y(s)-1 & =\frac{s+2}{{s}^{2}+4}\end{aligned}
$$

We rearrange to solve for $Y(s).$ First, add $1$ to the right-hand side and find a common denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}(s+3)Y(s) & =1+\frac{s+2}{{s}^{2}+4} \\ (s+3)Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}+4}{{s}^{2}+4}+\frac{s+2}{{s}^{2}+4} \\ (s+3)Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}+s+6}{{s}^{2}+4}\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing by $(s+3),$ we obtain

$$
Y(s)=\frac{{s}^{2}+s+6}{(s+3)({s}^{2}+4)}.
$$

Next, we perform a partial fraction decomposition. Since the denominator has a linear factor $(s+3)$ and an irreducible quadratic factor $({s}^{2}+4),$ we write

$$
\frac{{s}^{2}+s+6}{(s+3)({s}^{2}+4)}=\frac{A}{s+3}+\frac{Bs+C}{{s}^{2}+4}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
{s}^{2}+s+6=A({s}^{2}+4)+(Bs+C)(s+3)
$$

- Setting $s=-3,$ we have
 

$$
(-3)^{2}+(-3)+6=A((-3)^{2}+4)+0\,⟹\,12=13A\,⟹\,A=\frac{12}{13}.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of ${s}^{2},$ we have
  

$$
1=A+B\,⟹\,1=\frac{12}{13}+B\,⟹\,B=\frac{1}{13}.
$$

- Comparing the constant terms, we have
 

$$
6=4A+3C\,⟹\,6=4(\frac{12}{13})+3C\,⟹\,C=\frac{10}{13}.
$$

Thus, the decomposition is

$$
Y(s)=\frac{(\frac{12}{13})}{13(s+3)}+\frac{(\frac{1}{13}s+\frac{10}{13})}{{s}^{2}+4}=\frac{12}{13(s+3)}+\frac{s+10}{13({s}^{2}+4)}.
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+3}} & ={e}^{-3t} \\ {L}^{-1}{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2t \\ {L}^{-1}{\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking the inverse Laplace transform of $Y(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =\frac{12}{13}{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+3}}+\frac{1}{13}{L}^{-1}{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}}+\frac{5}{13}{L}^{-1}{\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}} \\ y(t) & =\frac{12}{13}{e}^{-3t}+\frac{5}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+\frac{1}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: At a geological site, an object is found with $75%$ of its original chlorine-36 content. Given that the half-life of chlorine-36 is $301$ thousand years, approximately how old is the object?
questions.worked_solution:
The mass $M(t)$ of a radioactive substance at time $t$ can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
{M}^{′}(t)=-kM(t),\,M(0)={M}_{0}.
$$

The general solution to this equation is

$$
M(t)={M}_{0}{e}^{-kt}.
$$

The half-life ${t}_{1/2}$ is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

$$
{t}_{1/2}=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}.
$$

Since we know that ${t}_{1/2}=301$ thousand years, we have

$$
301=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}\,⇒\,k=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{301}.
$$

So, we have

$$
M(t)={M}_{0}{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/301}.
$$

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t)=0.75{M}_{0}.$ So, we set up our equation as follows:

$$
0.75{M}_{0}={M}_{0}{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/301}
$$

Solving this equation for $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}0.75{M}_{0} & ={M}_{0}{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/301} \\ 0.75\cancel{{M}_{0}} & =\cancel{{M}_{0}}{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/301} \\ 0.75 & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/301} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.75) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/301}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.75) & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{301} \\ t & =-\frac{301\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.75)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ t & ≈125.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the object is approximately $125$ thousand years old.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Terminal Velocity
questions.problem:
An object of mass $20\,\text{kg}$ falls vertically downward. Let $v$ be its velocity, with downward taken as the positive direction.
The air resistance on the object is proportional to the square of its velocity and acts in the opposite direction to the direction of motion.
At a particular moment during the fall, the object's velocity is $\sqrt{3}\,\text{m/s}$ and its instantaneous acceleration is $\frac{147}{40}\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

What is the terminal velocity ${v}_{\text{term}}$ of the object? Assume the acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2},$ and the only forces acting on the object are the weight due to gravity and drag. 

Express your answer in the form $a\sqrt{b},$ where $a$ and $b$ are rational numbers.

${v}_{\text{term}}=$
{{field-1}}
$\text{m/s}$
questions.worked_solution:
Terminal velocity is the constant speed a falling object approaches as the upward resistive force (drag) grows to exactly balance the downward gravitational force.
That is, at terminal velocity (a constant), acceleration is zero, so by $F=ma,$ the resultant force is zero.

First, note that only two forces act on the object: the force due to gravity, given by the weight

$$
w=mg=20\cdot 9.8=196\,\text{N},
$$

and the force due to drag $D,$ which is proportional to the square of the velocity (and negative since it acts in the negative direction),

$$
D=-k{v}^{2},
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality. Hence, the resultant force acting on the object is

$$
F=w+D=196-k{v}^{2}.
$$

Applying Newton's second law, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\ 196-k{v}^{2} & =20a\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that, at a particular moment, the object's velocity is $\sqrt{3}\,\text{m/s}$ and its instantaneous acceleration is $\frac{147}{40}\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Substituting these values into the above, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}196-k\cdot {(\sqrt{3})}^{2} & =20\cdot \frac{147}{40} \\ 196-3k & =\frac{147}{2} \\ -3k & =-\frac{245}{2} \\ k & =\frac{245}{6}\,\text{kg/m}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the resultant force acting on the object is

$$
F=196-\frac{245}{6}{v}^{2}.
$$

When the object reaches terminal velocity ${v}_{\text{term}},$ the resultant force is zero:

$$
196-\frac{245}{6}({v}_{\text{term}})^{2}=0\,⟹\,{v}_{\text{term}}=\sqrt{\frac{24}{5}}=\frac{2\sqrt{30}}{5}
$$

Therefore, the terminal velocity of the object is ${v}_{\text{term}}=\frac{2\sqrt{30}}{5}\,\text{m/s}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining an Amount at an Overflow Point
questions.problem: A saline reservoir for a medical research lab can hold up to $160\,\text{gal}$ of solution. Initially, it contains $100\,\text{gal}$ of saline solution with $25\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved salt. A more concentrated saline solution with concentration $1.0\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the reservoir at a rate of $6\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $4\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of salt in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow.
questions.worked_solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the reservoir at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which salt enters the reservoir minus the rate at which salt leaves the reservoir.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the reservoir.

First, note that a solution containing $1.0\,\text{lb/gal}$ of salt enters the reservoir at a rate of $6\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the reservoir is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(1.0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (6\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(1.0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (6\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =6\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which salt leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $100\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $6\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $4\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=100+6t-4t=2(50+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{2(50+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $4\,\text{gal/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(4\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{2(50+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(4\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{2(50+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{4Q}{2(50+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{50+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =6-\frac{2Q}{50+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{50+t}\,Q=6.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(50+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|50+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(50+t)^{2}} \\  & =(50+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(50+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(50+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{50+t}\,Q) & =(50+t)^{2}\cdot 6 \\ (50+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(50+t)Q & =6(50+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(50+t)^{2}) & =6(50+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(50+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 6(50+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(50+t)^{2} & =6\cdot \frac{1}{3}(50+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =2(50+t)+\frac{C}{(50+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $25\,\text{lb}$ of salt. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=25,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =25 \\ 2(50+0)+\frac{C}{(50+0)^{2}} & =25 \\ 100+\frac{C}{(50)^{2}} & =25 \\ \frac{C}{(50)^{2}} & =-75 \\ C & =-75(50)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =2(50+t)-\frac{75(50)^{2}}{(50+t)^{2}} \\  & =2(50+t)-75{(\frac{50}{50+t})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reservoir begins to overflow. The reservoir has a capacity of $160\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=160$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =160 \\ 100+6{t}_{o}-4{t}_{o} & =160 \\ 100+2{t}_{o} & =160 \\ 2{t}_{o} & =60 \\ {t}_{o} & =30\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of salt in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(30) & =2(50+30)-75{(\frac{50}{50+30})}^{2} \\  & =160-75{(\frac{50}{80})}^{2} \\  & ≈130.7\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A dye mixing tank at a textile factory can hold up to $180\,\text{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $100\,\text{gal}$ of solution with $20\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved dye. A more concentrated dye solution with concentration $0.6\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of dye in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow.
questions.worked_solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of dye in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which dye enters the tank minus the rate at which dye leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which dye enters the tank.

First, note that a solution containing $0.6\,\text{lb/gal}$ of dye enters the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *dye* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.6\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.6\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =9\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which dye exits the tank.

To find the rate at which dye leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $100\,\text{gal}$ of liquid; solution enters at $15\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $10\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=100+15t-10t=5(20+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of dye in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{5(20+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min},$ *dye* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(10\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(10\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{10Q}{5(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{20+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =9-\frac{2Q}{20+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{20+t}\,Q=9.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(20+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|20+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(20+t)^{2}} \\  & =(20+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(20+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(20+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{20+t}\,Q) & =(20+t)^{2}\cdot 9 \\ (20+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(20+t)Q & =9(20+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(20+t)^{2}) & =9(20+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(20+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 9(20+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(20+t)^{2} & =9\cdot \frac{1}{3}(20+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =3(20+t)+\frac{C}{(20+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $20\,\text{lb}$ of dye. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=20,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =20 \\ 3(20+0)+\frac{C}{(20+0)^{2}} & =20 \\ 60+\frac{C}{(20)^{2}} & =20 \\ \frac{C}{(20)^{2}} & =-40 \\ C & =-40(20)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =3(20+t)-\frac{40(20)^{2}}{(20+t)^{2}} \\  & =3(20+t)-40{(\frac{20}{20+t})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $180\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=180$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =180 \\ 100+15{t}_{o}-10{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 100+5{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 5{t}_{o} & =80 \\ {t}_{o} & =16\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of dye in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(16) & =3(20+16)-40{(\frac{20}{20+16})}^{2} \\  & =108-40{(\frac{20}{36})}^{2} \\  & ≈95.7\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
For which of the following values is the implicit Euler method stable, given that $\lambda $ is the parameter of the test equation?

- $\lambda Δx=0.1$
- $\lambda Δx=0.8$
- $\lambda Δx=1.2$
- $\lambda Δx=5$

*Hint: The stability function $R$ of the implicit Euler method is given by*

$$
R(\lambda Δx)=\frac{1}{1+\lambda Δx}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A numerical method 
${y}_{n+1}={y}_{n}+Δ{y}_{n}$
is stable for a given step size $Δx$ if, when applied to the test equation

$$
{y}^{′}=-\lambda y,\,y(0)=1,\,x\ge 0,\,\lambda >0,
$$

the numerical solution satisfies ${y}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty ,$ just like the exact solution.

When a method is applied to the test equation, the update takes the form

$$
{y}_{n+1}=R(\lambda Δx){y}_{n},
$$

where $R(\lambda Δx)$ is referred to as the stability function of the method. The set of values for which the method is stable, given by $|R(\lambda Δx)|<1,$ is called the stability region of the method.

The stability function of the implicit Euler method is

$$
R(\lambda Δx)=\frac{1}{1+\lambda Δx}.
$$

Let's check the stability of the implicit Euler Method for each of the given values in turn.

- For $\lambda Δx=0.1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(0.1)| & =|\frac{1}{1+0.1}| \\  & =|\frac{1}{1.1}| \\  & =0.9090…<1.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Since this value falls *within* the stability region, the implicit Euler method is stable.

- For $\lambda Δx=0.8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(0.8)| & =|\frac{1}{1+0.8}| \\  & =|\frac{1}{1.8}| \\  & =0.5555…<1.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Since this value falls *within* the stability region, the implicit Euler method is stable.

- For $\lambda Δx=1.2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(1.2)| & =|\frac{1}{1+1.2}| \\  & =|\frac{1}{2.2}| \\  & =0.4545…<1.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Since this value falls *within* the stability region, the implicit Euler method is stable.

- For $\lambda Δx=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(5)| & =|\frac{1}{1+5}| \\  & =|\frac{1}{6}| \\  & =0.1666…<1.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Since this value falls *within* the stability region, the implicit Euler method is stable.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, III, and IV".

Note that, since the implicit Euler method is absolutely stable, it is stable for all possible values of $\lambda Δx.$

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=x-{y}^{3},\,y(0)=1
$$

Use the trapezoidal method with one step and Newton's method to approximate $y(1).$ Round your answer to two decimal places.

$y(1)≈$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

Since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=1,$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=1-0=1.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the trapezoidal method. In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((x-{y}^{3})+({x}_{\text{new}}-({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}))\cdot 1 \\  & =0.5x-0.5{y}^{3}+0.5{x}_{\text{new}}-0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+0.5x-0.5{y}^{3}+0.5{x}_{\text{new}}-0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3},\end{aligned}
$$

and moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}+0.5{y}^{3}-y-0.5{x}_{\text{new}}-0.5x=0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=1$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}+0.5{y}^{3}-y-0.5{x}_{\text{new}}-0.5x.
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=0+1=1.
$$

 Then, the function $g$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}+0.5(1)^{3}-1-0.5\cdot 1-0.5\cdot 0 \\  & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

We use a root-finding method with starting point $y=1$ to solve $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.$ We'll use Newton's method:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{g({y}_{\text{new}})}{{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})}.
$$

Note that the derivative of $g$ is

$$
{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})=1.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+1.
$$

Therefore, our Newton's method iterative scheme is as follows:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{0.5(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{3}+({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-1}{1.5(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{2}+1}.
$$

Applying several iterations of Newton's method starting with $y(0)=1,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}({y}_{\text{new}})_{1} & =1 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{2} & =0.8 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{3} & ≈0.771\,429 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{4} & ≈0.770\,917\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $y(1)≈0.77,$ rounded to two decimal places.

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4x+2y}.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|g(x,y)|=4y-C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2(2x+y)}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2 & =\frac{1}{2z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{4z+1}{2z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2z}{4z+1}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{2z}{4z+1}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}\int (1-\frac{1}{4z+1})\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}(z-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|4z+1|) & =x+K \\ 4z-\operatorname{ln}⁡|4z+1| & =8x+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=8K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}8x+4y-\operatorname{ln}⁡|8x+4y+1| & =8x+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|8x+4y+1| & =4y-C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
g(x,y)=8x+4y+1.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1-3\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-2y).
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=6x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1-3\operatorname{sec}⁡(2(x-y))\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=x-y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1-3\operatorname{sec}⁡(2z)\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=3\operatorname{sec}⁡(2z).
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2z)\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =3 \\ \int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2z)\,\text{d}z & =\int 3\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2z) & =3x+K \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2z) & =6x+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=2K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-2y)=6x+C
$$

Therefore, 

$$
g(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-2y).
$$

questions.problem:
$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}{y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0
$$

Let ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ be solutions to the second-order homogeneous differential equation above, where $Q(x)$ is continuous on $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ The Wronskian satisfies $W(0)=2.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.
The Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies the following first-order differential equation:

$$
{W}^{′}(x)={{field-1}}W(x)
$$

Solving this equation, we get

$$
W={{field-2}}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

Now, using the fact that $W(0)=2,$ we obtain 
{{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Abel's identity says that if ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions of

$$
{y}^{″}+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0,
$$

then their Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=-P(x)W(x).
$$

In our equation, the coefficient of ${y}^{′}$ is 

$$
P(x)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Substituting into Abel's identity gives

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}W(x).
$$

Now, we solve the first-order differential equation for $W:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}^{′} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}W \\ \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =\int -\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|W| & =-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+K \\ |W| & ={e}^{K}{e}^{-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)} \\ W & =C{e}^{-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Next, we use the given value $W(0)=2$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W(0) & =C{e}^{-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0)} \\ 2 & =C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have $W(x)\ne 0\text{ for all }x\in R.$

choices.value: $W(x)=0$ for some but not all $x\in R$

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,

the $2$-Step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton (ABM $2$-step) Method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Predictor} & : & Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx, \\ \text{Corrector} & : & Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx,\end{aligned}
$$

where

- ${y}^{′}=f(x,y)$ is the estimated slope at the current point $(x,y),$

- ${y}_{-1}^{′}=f({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})$ is the estimated slope at the previous point (${x}_{-1},{y}_{-1}),$ and

- ${y}_{p}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})$ is the estimated slope at the predicted new point $({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})=(x+Δx,y+Δ{y}_{p}).$

Before we start, let's add the initial condition data and Runge-Kutta step data to a table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ |  | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Now, since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=2,$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=2-1=1.
$$

First, we compute the values of ${y}^{′}$ at each point according to the given rule:

- The slope at the previous point $({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})=(0,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{-1}^{′} & =2{x}_{-1}-2{y}_{-1}-3 \\  & =2\cdot 0-2\cdot 1-3 \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

- The slope at the current point $(x,y)=(1,0)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2x-2y-3 \\  & =2\cdot 1-2\cdot 0-3 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ |  |  |  |  |

Next, we compute $Δ{y}_{p}$ using the predictor equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\cdot (-1)-(-5))\cdot 1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ |  |  |  |

So, the coordinates of the predicted new point are

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+1=2, \\ {y}_{p} & =y+Δ{y}_{p}=0+1=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add the second value to the table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $1$ |  |  |

Hence, the slope at this predicted point is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =2{x}_{\text{new}}-2{y}_{p}-3 \\  & =2\cdot 2-2\cdot 1-3 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-1$ |  |

Finally, we compute $Δy$ using the corrector equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(5\cdot (-1)+8\cdot (-1)-(-5))\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot (-8) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-\frac{2}{3}$ |

The value of $x$ in the next row is ${x}_{\text{new}}=2.$ To get the value of $y$ in the next row, we add $Δy$ to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\  & =0+(-\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these results to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-\frac{2}{3}$ |
| $2$ | $-\frac{2}{3}$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that $y(2)≈-\frac{2}{3}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Approximating the Solution to a Second-Order ODE Using Euler's Method With Two Steps
questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}-y=0,\,y(1)=-1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=2
$$

Use Euler's Method with two steps to approximate $y(2)$ and ${y}^{′}(2).$

$$
y(2)≈{{field-1}},\,{y}^{′}(2)≈{{field-2}}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}=f(x,y,{y}^{′}),\,y(a)=c,\,{y}^{′}(a)=d,
$$

we can use Euler's method to approximate a solution by first reducing the second-order ODE to a system of first-order ODEs,

$$
{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=z,\, & y(a)=c, \\ {z}^{′}=f(x,y,z)\, & z(a)=d,\end{aligned}
$$

before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation.

To apply Euler’s method, we first isolate ${y}^{″}$ so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}-y & =0 \\ {x}^{2}{y}^{″} & =y-4{y}^{′} \\ {y}^{″} & =\frac{y-4{y}^{′}}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute our new variable $z={y}^{′},{z}^{′}={y}^{″}$ in the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{z}^{′}=\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}}.
$$

Note that the initial value of $z$ is $z(1)={y}^{′}(1)=2.$
So, the initial value problem reduces to the following system of first-order ODEs:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=z,\, & y(1)=-1, \\ {z}^{′}=\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}},\, & z(1)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can proceed with Euler's method by applying the update rule component-wise.

First, note that we are given the values of $y$ and $z={y}^{′}$ at $x=1$ and asked to find their values at $x=2.$ The distance from $x=1$ to $x=2$ is $1,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be

$$
Δx=\frac{2-1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, we'll start by creating a table that includes the initial condition data $y(1)=-1$ and $z(1)=2.$

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ |  |  | $2$ |  |  |

**Step 1**.

We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy,$ ${z}^{′}$ and $Δz$ (using the values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the first row), and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}},$ ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=2 \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{-1-4\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}}=-9 \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=2\cdot \frac{1}{2}=1 \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx=-9\cdot \frac{1}{2}=-\frac{9}{2} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=-1+1=0 \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=2-\frac{9}{2}=-\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-9$ | $-\frac{9}{2}$ |
| $\frac{3}{2}$ | $0$ |  |  | $-\frac{5}{2}$ |  |  |

**Step 2**.

We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy,$ ${z}^{′}$ and $Δz$ (using the values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the second row), and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}},$ ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=-\frac{5}{2} \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{0-4(-\frac{5}{2})}{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}}=\frac{10}{(\frac{9}{4})}=\frac{40}{9} \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=-\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}=-\frac{5}{4} \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx=\frac{40}{9}\cdot \frac{1}{2}=\frac{20}{9} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=2 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=0-\frac{5}{4}=-\frac{5}{4} \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=-\frac{5}{2}+\frac{20}{9}=-\frac{5}{18}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-9$ | $-\frac{9}{2}$ |
| $\frac{3}{2}$ | $0$ | $-\frac{5}{2}$ | $-\frac{5}{4}$ | $-\frac{5}{2}$ | $\frac{40}{9}$ | $\frac{20}{9}$ |
| $2$ | $-\frac{5}{4}$ |  |  | $-\frac{5}{18}$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that
$y(2)≈-\frac{5}{4}$
and
${y}^{′}(2)=z(2)≈-\frac{5}{18}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Writing a Homogeneous ODE as a Matrix Differential Equation
questions.problem:
The second-order differential equation $2{y}^{″}+{y}^{′}-3y=0$
can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where 

$$
x(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}],\,y(t)={x}_{1}(t),\,{y}^{′}(t)={x}_{2}(t).
$$

Find the matrix $A.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{′}+\frac{3}{2}y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}+\frac{3}{2}{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=\frac{3}{2}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ \frac{3}{2} & -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Hence, $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ \frac{3}{2} & -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}].$

questions.knowledge_point: Fully Classifying Recurrence Relations
questions.problem:
Classify the recurrence relation

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{n-3}-{a}_{n-1},\,{a}_{1}={a}_{2}={a}_{3}=1,\,n\ge 4.
$$

The recurrence relation ${a}_{n}$ has order
{{field-1}},
is
{{field-2}},
and is
{{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following classifications of recurrence relations:

- The order of a relation ${a}_{n}$ is the largest index difference between ${a}_{n}$ and the preceding terms in the relation.

- A recurrence relation is *linear (with constant coefficients)* if it expresses ${a}_{n}$ as a sum of previous terms ${a}_{n-1},…,{a}_{n-k}$ with constant coefficients, together with possibly a final term that depends only on $n:$

$$
{a}_{n}={s}_{1}{a}_{n-1}+{s}_{2}{a}_{n-2}+…+{s}_{k}{a}_{n-k}+g(n)
$$

where ${s}_{1},{s}_{2},…,{s}_{k}$ are constants and $g(n)$ is a function, often called a *forcing function*, that does not involve ${a}_{n}$ or its preceding terms.

- A linear recurrence relation (with constant coefficients) is *homogeneous* if the forcing function is zero. Otherwise, it is *inhomogeneous.*

Let's classify the relation ${a}_{n}={a}_{n-3}-{a}_{n-1}.$

- The largest index difference between ${a}_{n}$ and the preceding terms ${a}_{n-1}$  and ${a}_{n-3}$ in the relation is $3.$ So, the relation has order $3.$

- The previous terms ${a}_{n-1},$ and ${a}_{n-3}$ occur only in the first power and their coefficients are constants. So, the relation is linear.

- The relation is linear, yet there is no forcing function (i.e., $g(n)=0$ for all $n$). So, the relation is homogeneous.

Therefore, the recurrence relation ${a}_{n}$ has order
$3,$
is
$\text{linear},$
and is
$\text{homogeneous}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Distance Between Two Objects
questions.problem:
The gravitational force between two objects, of masses $(4.5\times {10}^{6})\,\text{kg}$ and $(2.8\times {10}^{6})\,\text{kg},$ has a magnitude of $(3.6\times {10}^{-3})\,\text{N}.$
According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, what is the distance between the centers of mass of the two objects? Write your answer in scientific notation, rounding to **two significant figures** where appropriate. Assume the Newtonian constant of gravitation is $G=(6.67\times {10}^{-11})\,{\text{m}}^{3}/(\text{kg}\cdot {\text{s}}^{2}).$

The distance between the two objects is
$(${{field-1}}
$\times $
{{field-2}}$)\,\text{m}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Newton's law of universal gravitation states that the gravitational force attracting two objects is proportional to the product of the two masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers of mass:

$$
F=G\frac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

where

- $F$ is the gravitational force between the objects, measured in Newtons $(\text{N}),$

- $G=(6.67\times {10}^{-11})\,{\text{m}}^{3}/(\text{kg}\cdot {\text{s}}^{2})$ is the Newtonian constant of gravitation,

- ${m}_{1}$ and ${m}_{2}$ are the masses of the objects, measured in $\text{kg},$ and

- $r$ is the distance between their centers of mass, measured in $\text{m}.$

First, let's rearrange the formula to make $r$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =G\frac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{{r}^{2}} \\ {r}^{2} & =G\frac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{F} \\ r & =\sqrt{G\frac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{F}}\end{aligned}
$$

Choosing ${m}_{1}=(4.5\times {10}^{6})\,\text{kg}$ and ${m}_{2}=(2.8\times {10}^{6})\,\text{kg}$ and substituting in the other known values, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{2} & =(6.67\times {10}^{-11})\cdot \frac{(4.5\times {10}^{6})\cdot (2.8\times {10}^{6})}{3.6\times {10}^{-3}} \\  & =\frac{6.67\cdot 4.5\cdot 2.8}{3.6}\times \frac{{10}^{-11}\cdot {10}^{6}\cdot {10}^{6}}{{10}^{-3}} \\  & =23.345\times {10}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking the square root, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{23.345\times {10}^{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{23.345}\times \sqrt{{10}^{4}} \\  & =(4.8316…)\times {10}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounded to two significant figures, the distance between the two objects is
$(\,4.8\times {10}^{2}\,)\,\text{m}.$
